We must rearrange `nums` in place so that odd indices hold local maxima and even indices hold local minima: `nums[0] < nums[1] > nums[2] < nums[3] ...`. The key difficulty versus the easier Wiggle Sort I is that **duplicates** are allowed, so a simple adjacent swap fails (e.g. `[1,3,2,2,3,1]`). The guaranteed-valid answer means we can always separate values into a 'smaller half' and 'larger half' and interleave them so equal elements never touch at even/odd boundaries. With n up to 5·10⁴, an $O(n \log n)$ sort-based solution passes easily; the follow-up asks for $O(n)$ time via quickselect and $O(1)$ space via index mapping.

**Example 1:** `[1,5,1,1,6,4]` → sorted `[1,1,1,4,5,6]`. Smaller half `[1,1,1]` fills even slots right-to-left, larger half `[4,5,6]` fills odd slots right-to-left → `[1,6,1,5,1,4]`. Placing halves from opposite ends keeps duplicates of the median apart.

**Example 2:** `[1,3,2,2,3,1]` → sorted `[1,1,2,2,3,3]`. Interleaving gives `[2,3,1,3,1,2]`, where the two 2s sit at even indices 0 and 2 (separated by an odd slot) and likewise for the two 3s.
k: Fill even positions with the smaller half of sorted values and odd positions with the larger half.
Place elements from the largest to smallest within each half (right-to-left) so duplicate medians land on same-parity indices and never become adjacent.
Quickselect finds the median in O(n); virtual indexing maps i -> (1+2i) % (n|1) so the three-way partition writes directly into wiggle positions using O(1) extra space.

a.i: Sort a copy of the array. The first ⌈n/2⌉ values are small enough for even positions and the rest for odd positions. To keep duplicates of the median from becoming neighbors, fill positions from the back: assign sorted[i] to position (n|1 related) — concretely, put the smaller half into even indices right-to-left and the larger half into odd indices right-to-left. Then any run of equal values is spread across same-parity slots separated by other values.
s: Let m = (n + 1) / 2 be the size of the smaller half.
For i from m-1 down to 0, write sorted[i] into nums[2*i].
For i from n-1 down to m, write sorted[i] into nums[2*(i-m)+1].
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting dominates; the interleaving pass is linear.
a.sp: O(n) — a sorted copy of the array.

a.n: Approach 2: Quickselect Median + Three-Way Partition with Virtual Indexing (O(n), O(1))
a.i: Find the median with quickselect ($O(n)$ average). Then do a three-way Dutch-flag partition around the median, but write through a **virtual index map**: real index `i` maps to `(1 + 2*i) % (n | 1)`, which enumerates all odd indices first, then all even indices. Partitioning so that large values go to low virtual indices (odd slots) and small ones to high virtual indices (even slots) yields the wiggle order directly in place. Using nth_element / quickselect plus this mapping achieves average $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ space.
s: Find the median value with quickselect (or C++ nth_element) on nums.
Define A(i) = (1 + 2*i) % (n | 1): the virtual-to-real index map visiting odds then evens.
Run Dutch-flag partition over virtual indices: if nums[A(i)] > median swap to front region, if < median swap to back region, else advance.
After partitioning, all greater-than-median values occupy odd slots, smaller-or-equal occupy even slots, satisfying the wiggle property.
a.t: O(n) average — quickselect is linear on average; the partition pass is linear. Worst case O(n²) without median-of-medians pivot selection.
a.sp: O(1) extra — partitioning happens in place through the virtual index map (the Java/JS versions use O(n) only because they sort a copy to get the median; a true quickselect removes that).

w:
**Which approach to use:** In an interview, start with Approach 1 (sort + reverse-interleave) — it's simple, clearly correct, and shows you understand why filling right-to-left handles duplicates. If asked the follow-up, present Approach 2: quickselect for the median plus Dutch-flag partitioning through the virtual index map `(1+2i) % (n|1)`.

**Common pitfalls:**
- Filling left-to-right from the sorted array places duplicate medians adjacently (e.g. `[4,5,5,6]` → wrong); always fill from the ends inward.
- Forgetting that the median's duplicates may appear in both halves — the parity trick (odds get strictly-greater side, evens get the rest) resolves it.
- Off-by-one in the virtual index map: use `(n | 1)` (round n up to odd) so the cycle covers all indices exactly once.

**Edge cases:** single element (already valid), two elements (`a < b` guaranteed by problem statement), all-equal arrays won't occur since a valid answer is guaranteed.

**Likely follow-ups:** prove correctness of the virtual index ordering; implement median-of-medians for worst-case O(n); adapt to Wiggle Sort I (non-strict inequalities allow a one-pass greedy swap).
